title: A Quantum Model for Constrained Markowitz Modern Portfolio Using Slack Variables to Process Mixed-Binary Optimization under QAOA
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a quantum formulation of constrained Markowitz portfolio optimization that embeds slack variables as ancilla qubits in the problem Hamiltonian, converting inequality constraints into an internalized QUBO suitable for QAOA. Simulation results on small instances show the slack-ancilla approach reliably finds the true optimal portfolio where standard penalty-based QAOA can fail, and the authors additionally conjecture a quantum lower bound on the joint precision of portfolio risk and return.
methodology_description: The paper adapts the classical Markowitz mean–variance portfolio optimization into a quantum-friendly QUBO/Ising formulation by introducing nonnegative slack variables to convert inequality constraints (ω_i ≤ α_i) into equalities (ω_i − α_i + s_i = 0). Each slack variable is encoded as a dedicated ancilla qubit (slack-ancilla scheme) and the resulting penalized objective (including β ∑(ω_i − α_i + s_i)^2) is mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian via ω_i ↦ (1 − Z_i)/2. A QAOA variational ansatz with depth p = 2 is used: alternating phase-separation unitaries U_H(γ) = exp(−i γ H) and mixer unitaries U_M(β) = exp(−i β Σ X_i), with variational angles θ = (γ_1, γ_2, β_1, β_2). The authors run noiseless statevector simulations (Qiskit) of the circuit, compute expectation values ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩, and optimize parameters in a classical outer loop using classical optimizers (Powell’s method and COBYLA are both reported). The penalty weight β is initialized at 1e2 and doubled every 20 Powell iterations until 100% feasibility is observed in a batch of 1000 samples, with a cap of 200 classical optimization steps per instance. Experiments use small synthetic 3-asset instances (n = 3) and compare the slack-ancilla QAOA to a standard penalty-based QAOA baseline and to a classical optimizer / ground-truth exhaustive solution.
frameworks: IBM Quantum Lab (cloud environment for experiments)
experimental_setup: Noiseless statevector simulation via Qiskit on IBM Quantum Lab. Small-scale experiments with n = 3 asset qubits plus one ancilla qubit per slack variable; QAOA depth p = 2. Classical optimization loop (Powell and/or COBYLA) run on a classical CPU. Penalty β scheduling: start at 1e2 and double every 20 Powell iterations until feasibility.
dataset_used: Synthetic three-asset portfolios. For each instance: µ ∈ R^3 sampled uniformly in [0.01, 0.10]; covariance Σ = L L^T with L lower-triangular and entries i.i.d. N(0, 0.05) (ensures positive-definiteness); α is a one-hot mask with exactly K = 1 active asset chosen uniformly at random.
experiment_input: Source: synthetically generated as described above. Size: n = 3 assets per instance; experiments repeated across 3 independent random seeds (distinct draws of µ, Σ, α). Preprocessing: none beyond sampling; slack variables mapped to ancilla qubits and penalty terms implemented via controlled-phase subcircuits.
experiment_process: 1) Generate synthetic instance (µ, Σ, α) for n=3. 2) Introduce slack variables s_i and form penalized objective with β ∑(ω_i − α_i + s_i)^2. 3) Map binary variables to Ising operators via ω_i ↦ (1−Z_i)/2 to produce Hamiltonian H with ZZ interactions and single-qubit Z fields. 4) Construct QAOA ansatz of depth p=2: apply alternating U_H(γ_k) and U_M(β_k) layers (k=1..2). 5) Simulate noiseless statevector via Qiskit to obtain ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩. 6) Optimize variational angles θ (and tuning penalty β via outer loop) using classical optimizers (Powell’s method and/or COBYLA). 7) Penalty schedule: initialize β=1e2 and double every 20 Powell iterations until 100% feasibility in a batch of 1000 samples or until 200 optimization steps reached. 8) Repeat across 3 random seeds and compare outputs to ground-truth exhaustive search and a penalty-only QAOA baseline.
experiment_output: Outputs are bitstring portfolio selections (binary vector indicating chosen assets), associated objective values (portfolio value corresponding to the mean–variance objective with penalties), and feasibility statistics (fraction of samples satisfying constraints). Baselines: exhaustive classical ground truth and standard penalty-based QAOA. Example reported results for one instance: ground-truth optimal [1,0,0] value 0.0468; standard penalty QAOA returned feasible but suboptimal [0,0,1] value 0.0376; slack-ancilla QAOA returned optimal [1,0,0] value 0.0468.

results_summary: The paper proposes a slack-ancilla method that embeds slack variables as ancilla qubits in the QAOA Hamiltonian to turn inequality constraints into equality constraints and thus internalize feasibility in the quantum state. The authors derive an Ising Hamiltonian for the penalized mean–variance portfolio problem, implement a one-ancilla-per-slack encoding and controlled-phase penalty subcircuits, and run noiseless statevector simulations on 3-asset instances. In these small simulations the slack-ancilla QAOA recovered the classical optimal portfolio while a standard penalty-based QAOA produced a different, suboptimal feasible portfolio. The paper additionally posits a theoretical conjecture linking quantum uncertainty-type bounds to a trade-off between portfolio risk and return. Claims of large practical speedups, reduced penalty magnitudes, and scalability are made but remain speculative based on the provided evidence.
performance_claims: Ground truth (classical exhaustive search) for one 3-asset instance: optimal portfolio [1, 0, 0] with objective value 0.0468.
Standard penalty-based QAOA (p = 2) for the same instance returned portfolio [0, 0, 1] with objective value 0.0376 (feasible but suboptimal).
Proposed slack-ancilla QAOA returned portfolio [1, 0, 0] with objective value 0.0468, matching ground truth on the tested instance.

Methodological assertion (claimed): required penalty strength β can be reduced by an order of magnitude (from 10^4 to 10^3) when using the slack-ancilla embedding (presented as a methodological benefit, not exhaustively benchmarked).

Methodological/time claim (claimed): 'Full feasibility is achieved at depth p = 2 on just three system qubits (plus ancillas), with 100% feasible portfolios in under one second of statevector simulation—compared to minutes for comparable classical solvers.'

Experimental protocol note: penalty weight β initialized at 10^2 and doubled every 20 Powell-optimizer iterations until 100% feasibility observed in a batch of 10^3 samples (used in simulation experiments).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports that the slack-ancilla QAOA matched the classical optimum on a 3-asset noiseless simulation and that a penalty-only QAOA produced a suboptimal solution in that toy instance. However, evidence is limited to small, noise-free simulations (n=3) with no hardware demonstrations, restricted benchmarking against classical methods, and no systematic scaling study. Therefore claims of a practical quantum advantage or large runtime improvements are speculative based on the presented results.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Slack-ancilla QAOA encoding internalizes inequality constraints by mapping slack variables to ancilla qubits; in noiseless statevector simulations (n=3, p=2) this approach recovered the classical ground-truth optimum where a standard penalty-based QAOA produced a suboptimal feasible solution.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The method is hybrid: a QAOA variational ansatz (p=2) is paired with classical outer-loop optimizers (Powell, COBYLA) and a penalty-scheduling protocol (β doubling) to enforce feasibility.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrated with shallow circuits and small qubit counts (3 system qubits + 3 ancilla) indicating a NISQ-oriented design, though only evaluated in noiseless simulation.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments are noiseless statevector simulations (Qiskit); no noisy simulations or runs on real QPUs are reported.
#limitation:qubit-count — The slack-ancilla scheme requires one ancilla per slack variable, increasing qubit overhead; experiments are limited to very small instances (n=3).
#limitation:data-encoding — Converting inequalities into equalities via slack ancilla increases encoding complexity and circuit structure (controlled-phase subcircuits) which may impede scaling.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — No empirical validation on hardware or noisy backends; speculative claims (e.g., conjectured quantum lower bound) are not empirically supported.
